episodes.title: How Big A Deal Is Chinese Chip Smuggling Anyway?
episodes.about: After Jensen Huang’s fall at Nvidia, chip smuggling has gone from a niche policy worry to the center of a Washington fight. Cabinet members traded blame over who let a suspected smuggling operation slide, the Commerce Department announced a new rule to close a loophole that let Chinese companies rent American AI chips through data centers abroad, and meanwhile, a campaign to reinstate Huang as CEO is growing. To make sense of it all, we’re joined by Ben Buchanan, the first White House Special Advisor for AI under President Biden and the architect of the original chip export controls. Ben explains why he has long fought to convince Washington that chips are central to national security and to developing AI safely, and what Washington should do next.
episodes.why: Kevin Roose and Casey Newton on the Washington fight over chip smuggling after Huang's fall — cabinet blame-trading, a new Commerce rule closing the rent-American-chips-through-foreign-data-centers loophole, and Ben Buchanan, who architected the original export controls, on what should happen next.

episodes.title: Why the AI Kids Hate Astra 6.2
episodes.about: Early testers say OpenAI’s Astra 6.2 stops halfway through coding projects and cuts its writing so short it’s hard to follow. But with the cost per task down 35% on one benchmark, is OpenAI betting that helping millions of office workers get through their busywork matters more than winning over developers? In the headlines: Nvidia’s board says it won’t reinstate Jensen Huang, and a wave of outages raises questions about the rush to modernize aging systems.
episodes.why: OpenAI's Astra 6.2 is landing badly with early testers — it stops halfway through coding projects and trims its writing to stubs — but it cuts cost per task by 35%, and NLW asks whether OpenAI is now optimizing for office busywork over developers.

episodes.title: #253: How Runway Is Transforming Creative Work With AI Agents
episodes.about: Runway's small creative team couldn't keep up with paid ad demand. Producing 77 ad units a week meant pulling people off brand, research, and product work. So they built an AI agent to handle the versioning, and now produce roughly 900 ads a week with return on ad spend doubled. Mike Kaput talks with Jamie Umpherson, Runway's Chief Creative Officer, about how that agent became Runway Ads, how App Studio turns vibe coding into custom creative software, and why taste and point of view matter more than ever for creatives working with AI.
episodes.why: Runway's creative team built an agent to version their ads and went from 77 to roughly 900 units a week with return on ad spend doubled; CCO Jamie Umpherson explains how that internal tool became the Runway Ads product.

episodes.title: The Missing Layer for Personal AI | First Person Labs’ Ken Liu
episodes.about: AI agents are getting smarter, but every new agent still has to learn who you are. What if your preferences, priorities, relationships, and digital context could move with you instead? First Person Labs co-founder Ken Liu joins a16z’s Martin Casado and Joel de la Garza to introduce Second, a personal context layer designed to understand what you’re doing across your digital life and make that context available to the agents you choose. They discuss how Second can proactively connect information across conversations and applications, why protecting such personal data requires a different security architecture, and the longer-term vision of AI that doesn’t just respond to prompts, but understands enough context to know when and how to help.
episodes.why: First Person Labs' Second is a personal context layer meant to carry your preferences, relationships and digital context from agent to agent, so each new agent doesn't start from zero — Casado and de la Garza press Liu on the security architecture that would require.

episodes.title: ‘Did A.I. Break the Internet?’ and Other Things We’ve Worried About This Week
episodes.about: In recent days, a series of technical outages have grounded planes, closed bank accounts, shut us out of our email and generally created a sense that the world is either falling apart or being hacked, or maybe both. The New York Times reporters Karoun Demirjian, Dustin Volz and Zolan Kanno-Youngs explain what’s really going on and whether we can expect it to continue.
episodes.why: Discovery pick — The Daily is the New York Times' flagship news show, not an AI show; three of its reporters work through the week's outage wave — grounded planes, closed bank accounts, dead email — and whether the world is falling apart, being hacked, or both.
